en: The semblance of tautology (*punaruktavadābhāsa*) and *chekānuprāsa*—thus *anuprāsa* is threefold; then there is *lāṭānuprāsa* and *rūpaka*, which is fourfold.
"Simile (upamā), the Illuminator (dīpaka), and likewise the Exemplification by Correspondence (prativastūpamā)—
these alone are the ornaments of speech as proclaimed by some."
"Punaruktābhāsa" (semblance of tautology) consists of words with different forms that appear as if they were non-different entities;
whereas "Chekānuprāsa" (refined alliteration) occurs when two pairs of sounds produce a very similar utterance.

The mode of expression known as *paraṣā* consists of words joined with the letters *śa* and *ṣa*, with the conjunction of the letter *ra*, and with the *ṣṭa*-group (the sibilants), as well as those conjoined with *hl*, *hv*, *hy*, and so forth.
The wise consider that [speech] to be *upanāgarikā* which is joined with similar consonants (*sarūpa-saṃyoga*), with the final letters of the vargas at the head, and with the stops (*sparśa*).
Those whose intellects are refined praise the *grāmya* (rustic) style— described by the term "soft" (*komala*) according to its application with the remaining phonemes— in poetic compositions.
Poets always desire a separate alliteration (*anuprāsa*) for each of these three modes, provided that the arrangement of syllables and consonants is identical.
Even when there is no difference in the meaning of the essential form, repetition is desired as *lāṭānuprāsa* (alliteration) due to a different purpose,
whether it concerns words (*śabda*) or phrases (*pada*).
By virtue of abiding in two words, one of the two is as before;
because the other is independent, or because both depend upon a single word.
Through the application of both [types of] independent phrases,
it is divided in many ways by various distinctions, following the sequence of repeated verses.
When one word, due to a lack of connection through direct audition (śruti),
is joined with another word as its primary element by means of a secondary function (guṇavṛtti), that is indeed a metaphor (rūpaka).
Since its definition is established by both the literal word and the meaning of the word,
it [the metaphor] has as its object either the whole thing or it is partial (ekadeśavivartin).
Metaphor in the form of a garland (mālārūpaka) is said to have all things as its object,
or it may occur in a single part through the representation [of that part] by means of another form.

They know that as *dīpaka* (illuminator) wherein the objects of the beginning, middle, and end are connected to both the primary and the secondary, with the qualities of comparison included within them.
When there is a similarity that captivates the mind between the object of comparison and the standard of comparison,
yet their respective words differ in terms of tense and so forth, that is indeed *upamā* (simile).

Just as that [comparison] deserves syntactic connection through direct audition (*śruti*) by virtue of its connection with the word *yathā*, it is stated to be of two kinds: [one] through association with words such as *sadṛśa* ("similar"), and [the other] otherwise.
Although this [simile] has been explained in brief by those who speak of its equivalence,
it is also formulated through the separation of the common property, the object of comparison, and their respective designators.

When both the object of comparison and the standard of comparison are expressed, that [simile] occurs; it may occur in a compound through the exclusion of the word expressing similarity, or sometimes even without that word expressing similarity. (UK 1.18)
Likewise, by means of comparison, through the force of the *ācārakyaṅ* affix, and by way of verbal expression,
that [comparison] sometimes occurs as the agent’s manner of acting (*ācāra*) with the suffix *kyaṅ*, and sometimes it occurs with the suffix *kvip*.

When the suffix *ṇamul* follows a word denoting an object or an agent in comparison—such as in *kaṣādam*—that [object] is expressed by the suffix *-vat*, which denotes a commonality with respect to the object. (UKSS 1.20)
When a suffix such as *vat* is added to a noun ending in the sixth or seventh case to denote that very object,
it is employed by poets along with other secondary suffixes (*taddhita*) such as *kalpa* and the like.

Where, in the proximity of a standard of comparison (*upamāna*), a word expressing similarity is uttered by the wise, and [where] the object of comparison (*upameya*) is [also expressed], that is called *prativastūpamā* (simile by parallelism) by poets. (UK 1.22)

Due to the established status of one as the contextual subject and the other as its opposite, one attains the state of being the object of comparison (upameya) while the other attains the state of being the standard of comparison (upamāna);
thus, there is an absence of any explicit word denoting comparison.

Others recognize the following as poetic ornaments (alaṃkāra): Paronomasia (ākṣepa), Corroboration by another matter (arthāntaranyāsa), Contrast (vyatireka), Peculiar Causation (vibhāvanā), Elliptical Exaggeration (samāsokti), and Hyperbole (atiśayokti).
Wise poets always declare that "Paranomasia" (ākṣepa) is a semblance of negation employed with the desire to express a particular distinction.
That [object], which is the subject matter of what is yet to be said and what has already been said, is held to be of two kinds;
its connection is declared to be by means of negation as well as by means of a positive injunction.

That which occurs before the statement of the proponent, or after that of another, or which occurs in reverse order, or through the use of the word *hi*, or otherwise; [that is a *vākya-antara*]. (UK 2.4)
This should be known as *arthāntaranyāsa* (corroboration by a general principle),
which stands distinct from *aprastutapraśaṃsā* (indirect praise) and *dṛṣṭānta* (simile), because it serves to corroborate the subject at hand.
When there is a specific attribute attributed to both the standard of comparison and the object of comparison,
that distinction (vyatireka) is of two kinds, according to whether the cause [of the difference] is unperceived or perceived.
That example which is presented by way of dissimilarity (vaidharmya) and is endowed with words such as "just as" (yathā) and "like" (iva)—
that too is accepted here as a negative concomitance (vyatireka), because it involves the application of a specific distinction.
When words suitable for a double entendre are cited separately,
the resulting production of a distinction is known as Vyatireka (Distinction).
When an action is prohibited, the manifestation of its result is to be known as "manifestation" (vibhāvanā) itself,
even though the means [to avoid it] are easily available.

The statement of an irrelevant matter (aprastutārtha) by means of a sentence whose primary sense is relevant, using qualifiers identical to those [of the relevant matter], is declared to be *samāsokti* (condensed expression).

But when the wise consider that which is based on signs (nimitta) yet has a sphere of activity transcending the world to be an expression of excellence (atiśayokti), they regard it as a poetic ornament (alaṃkāra).
Where non-difference is perceived despite difference, or where diversity is bound within what is otherwise,
such is the expression of *atiśayokti* (hyperbole) when based on a matter that is merely being imagined.
Where, due to a reversal of the sequence between cause and effect,
one is bound by relying upon the notion of simultaneity, that too is as explained before.

Furthermore, others state that for the ornamentation of speech, there are three additional figures of speech: yathāsaṃkhya (enumeration), utprekṣā (poetic fancy), and likewise svabhāvokti (description of intrinsic nature).
When there are many items taught that do not share the same grammatical case,
their subsequent explanation in successive order according to their respective numbers is called *yathāsaṃkhyam* (correspondence by number).

When there is no intention to express the form of identity, the figure of *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy), endowed with excellence, occurs through words such as *iva* and others, which denote the object itself, due to the connection with qualities or actions not belonging to that [object].

This imaginative construction (*utprekṣā*), which transcends the objects of the world due to the conceit of existence and non-existence, is expressed by [the poet] as if it were the literal meaning (*vācya*) itself.
The description of the natural disposition (*svabhāvokti*) of someone such as a young deer who is engaged in an action, serving as the basis for their various gestures, has been illustrated.

Others recognize the following ornaments: the Sweet (preyas), the Energetic (ūrjasvi), the Periphrastic (paryāyokta), the Resolved (samāhita), the Exalted (udātta) in its two forms, and the Pun (śliṣṭa).

That poetry which is composed by the wise through the indication of states such as love (*rati*) and others by means of their consequents (*anubhāva*) and so forth, is declared to be *preyas* (the pleasant).
This [drama] is flavorful, displaying clearly the erotic and other sentiments;
it is the locus for the direct expression of words, the permanent emotions, the transitory emotions, the determinants, and the dramatic representations.
In dramatic performance, nine aesthetic sentiments (rasas) are traditionally recognized: the erotic, the comic, the furious, the heroic, the terrible, the loathsome, the marvelous, and the peaceful.
The composition of mental states and aesthetic sentiments that proceed from impropriety due to causes such as desire, anger,
and so forth, is called the *ūrjasvin* (the forceful).
Paryāyokta (periphrasis) is that which is expressed by another means,
devoid of the functions of the expressed and the expressive, and consisting of comprehension.
That which consists of the cessation of the activity of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*), emotion (*bhāva*), and their semblances (*tadābhāsa*),
and whose nature is devoid of any other external excitants (*anubhāva*), is *samāhita*.
Exalted and prosperous subjects, as well as the deeds of great-souled beings,
have attained the status of illustrations and have not become mere historical narratives.
The conjunction of words uttered with a single effort, which bear their respective shadows and are distinguished by qualities such as the *svarita* accent, is here called *śliṣṭa* (punning).
Let that [poetry] which, through words generating a flash of genius (*pratibhā*) contained within other ornaments,
is distinguished by the expression of both meaning and sound, be recognized as such.

Apahnuti (concealment), Viśeṣokti (peculiar assertion), Virodha (contradiction), Tulyayogitā (equal pairing), Aprastutapraśaṃsā (indirect praise), Vyājastuti (disguised praise), and Vidarśanā (illustration).

Furthermore, others have declared these ornaments of speech to be: the comparison of the compared with the standard (upameyopamā), the expression of simultaneous action (sahokti), the blending of figures (saṃkara), and exchange (parivṛtti).
Apahnuti (concealment) is also desired as a form of internal simile;
its composition by the wise is carried out through the denial of a real fact.
When, despite the completeness of the causal complex, there is a restriction on the non-arising of the effect due to the powers [of the causes],
that statement intended to express a specific distinction is called a "statement of a particularity" (viśeṣokti).
Through the manifestation of signs and through the non-perception of signs,
her bondage is seen to be twofold in its graceful nature within the object of perception.
When a statement regarding an action contrary to either a quality or an action is made for the purpose of expressing a specific distinction, that they call "contradiction" (virodha).

*Tulyayogitā* (Equal Pairing) consists of speech that expresses similarity through subjects not under discussion—whether they are devoid of an explicit statement of comparison and its object, or whether they are relevant to the context. (UK 5.7)
The praise of another thing that has no connection to the subject at hand, yet which is linked to the matter under discussion, is this: Aprastutapraśaṃsā (Praise of the Irrelevant). // 5.8 //
Where, by the very nature of the power of words, censure is understood,
yet praise is intended in reality, that is considered "Praise in Disguise" (vyājastuti).
Where one imagines a relationship between things that either does not exist or does exist,
and expresses the state of being the object of comparison and the subject of comparison, that is called *vidarśanā*.
When multiple figures of speech are suggested simultaneously, and it is impossible for them to function together,
yet there is no logical reason to prefer one over the other, that is *saṃkara* (commixture).
When figures of speech based on both word and meaning appear together in a single sentence,
they are designated as "commixture" (saṃkara), whether by their coexistence or by their entry into a single component of the sentence.
Where figures of speech exist by means of mutual assistance and do not attain their own existence independently, that too is *saṃkara* (commixture).
Where there is a mutual relationship of the standard of comparison and the object of comparison,
they call that *upameyopamā* (reciprocal simile), which results in the rejection of other alternatives.
When two actions occurring at the same time and resting upon two objects are expressed by a single word, that is considered by the wise to be Sahokti (Conjoined Description).
But for some, there is a transformation [of things] through their common, deficient, or specific qualities;
that which consists in the nature of gain or loss is what was called "transformation" (parivṛtti).
Others recognize the following ornaments: Ananvaya (non-comparison), Sasaṃdeha (doubtful), Saṃsṛṣṭi (conjunction), Bhāvika, as well as Kāvyadṛṣṭānta (poetic illustration) and Hetu (cause).
Furthermore, when one speaks of both the true nature and the distinction by means of a simile,
the wise call that speech "sasaṃdeha" (full of doubt) for the purpose of praise.
That which, by casting the shadow of another figure of speech upon the intellect,
assumes the form of doubt even when there is no actual doubt, is called *saṃdeha* (doubt).
Where there is the relation of standard of comparison and object of comparison between that very same thing and itself,
because of the intended expression of non-similarity, they call that *ananvaya* (non-comparison).
The coexistence of many or even two figures of speech in a single locus,
when they are mutually independent of one another, is called "commingling" (saṃsṛṣṭi).
The *bhāvika* [figure of speech] occurs when past and future events, though most wondrous, appear as if directly perceived before one's eyes due to the lack of confusion in the expression of words.
When a single thing heard elsewhere serves as the cause for either a recollection or a direct experience, that is called *kāvyaliṅga* (poetic causation).
The wise define an example (dṛṣṭānta) as the clear illustration of a reflection of a desired object, devoid of words such as "just as" (yathā) and so forth.
